claim: parg-2 was significantly upregulated in neurons with activated DLK signaling (187-fold upregulated in dlk-1(OE) vs wild type, p<0.01).
source: The gene parg-2 (poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase-2) was significantly upregulated in neurons with activated DLK signaling (187-fold upregulated in dlk-1(OE) vs wild type, p<0.01, two-way ANOVA, Bonferroni post-test) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data presented in Figure 1A with statistical analysis (p<0.01, two-way ANOVA).

claim: parg-1 showed a 2.5-fold increase in the dlk-1(OE) background compared to wild type (p<0.05).
source: Further, examination of RNA-Seq results for the parg-2 paralog, parg-1, detected a 2.5-fold increase in the dlk-1(OE) background compared to wild type (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA, Bonferroni post-test, Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data presented in Figure 1A with statistical analysis (p<0.05, two-way ANOVA).

claim: Elevated expression of parg-1 and parg-2 by DLK signaling depended on the canonical DLK MAP kinase pathway since up-regulation was eliminated in neurons that over-expressed dlk-1 but lacked its downstream effector pmk-3.
source: Elevated expression of parg-1 and parg-2 by DLK signaling depended on the canonical DLK MAP kinase pathway since up-regulation was eliminated in neurons that over-expressed dlk-1 but lacked its downstream effector pmk-3 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data comparing dlk-1(OE) and dlk-1(OE); pmk-3(-) shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Up-regulation (>two fold, p<0.05) of gene expression by DLK signaling was observed for only 1.9% of coding genes (386 out of 20,375 protein coding genes assayed).
source: Overall, up-regulation (>two fold, p<0.05) (See Materials and methods) of gene expression by DLK signaling was observed for only 1.9% of coding genes (386 out of 20,375 protein coding genes assayed); expression of most genes was not affected by DLK signaling.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq analysis of 20,375 protein coding genes with statistical threshold (>2 fold, p<0.05).

claim: Expression levels of the pan-neuronal control gene rgef-1 were not altered in either mutant background.
source: For example, expression levels of the pan-neuronal control gene rgef-1 (a ras nucleotide exchange factor) were not altered in either mutant background (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data showing no change in rgef-1 expression in Figure 1A.

claim: parg expression is regulated by DLK signaling in GABA neurons.
source: Together, our data indicate parg expression is regulated by DLK signaling in GABA neurons.
evidence: Inferred from RNA-Seq data showing upregulation of parg-1 and parg-2 in dlk-1(OE) neurons.

claim: mCherry driven by the parg-2 promoter was detected in 90% of GABA neurons in dlk-1(OE) animals and 19% of GABA neurons in control animals (p<0.0001).
source: At high magnification (40X), mCherry was seen in 90% of GABA neurons in dlk-1(OE) animals and 19% of GABA neurons in control animals (Figure 1B,C) (p<0.0001, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data quantified in Figure 1B,C with statistical analysis (p<0.0001, Fisher's exact test).

claim: mCherry driven by the parg-2 promoter was not detected in dlk-1(lf) animals.
source: mCherry was not detected in dlk-1(lf) animals, which lack DLK-1.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy observations in dlk-1(lf) animals.

claim: parg-2 expression is dependent on dlk-1, even in intact, uninjured axons.
source: Therefore, parg-2 expression is dependent on dlk-1, even in intact, uninjured axons.
evidence: Inferred from reporter expression data showing parg-2 promoter activity requires dlk-1.

claim: Approximately 10 hr post-axotomy, parg-2 expression was significantly elevated in cut GABA axons relative to parg-2 expression in GABA axons of uninjured animals (47% vs 19%, p=0.0028).
source: Approximately 10 hr post-axotomy, parg-2 expression was significantly elevated in cut GABA axons relative to parg-2 expression in GABA axons of uninjured animals (47% vs 19%, p=0.0028, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data comparing injured and uninjured axons with statistical analysis (p=0.0028, Fisher's exact test).

claim: parg-2 expression increased in uninjured neurons neighboring injured neurons to equivalent levels as injured neurons (47% vs 41%, p=0.6722).
source: Further, by examining neighboring uncut GABA axons, we found that parg-2 expression also increased in uninjured neurons to equivalent levels (47% vs 41%, p=0.6722, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data comparing cut and neighboring uncut axons with statistical analysis (p=0.6722, Fisher's exact test).

claim: The increase in parg-2 expression in response to injury is entirely dependent on dlk-1, as parg-2 expression was not seen in cut or uncut axons in injured dlk-1(lf) animals.
source: The increase in parg-2 expression in response to injury is entirely dependent on dlk-1, as parg-2 expression was not seen in cut or uncut axons in injured dlk-1(lf) animals (p=0.0003 and p=0.0001, relative to cut axons and uncut axons in injured wild type animals).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data in dlk-1(lf) animals with statistical analysis (p=0.0003 and p=0.0001, Fisher's exact test).

claim: parg-2 expression is upregulated in injured neurons and their neighbors, and dependent on dlk-1.
source: Thus, parg-2 expression is upregulated in injured neurons and their neighbors, and dependent on dlk-1.
evidence: Inferred from reporter expression data in injured and neighboring neurons in wild type and dlk-1(lf) backgrounds.

claim: Poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolases (PARGs) catalyze dePARylation: the removal of the post-translational modification poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR) from target proteins.
source: Poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolases (PARGs) catalyze dePARylation: the removal of the post-translational modification poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR) from target proteins (Miwa and Sugimura, 1971; Althaus and Richter, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Miwa and Sugimura, 1971; Althaus and Richter, 1987).

claim: The parg-1 and parg-2 genes encode the only two PARGs in the C. elegans genome.
source: The parg-1 and parg-2 genes encode the only two PARGs in the C. elegans genome (Gagnon et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gagnon et al., 2002.

claim: Loss of parg-1 reduced axon regeneration to 39% compared to 70% in control animals.
source: Loss of either parg-1 or parg-2 reduced axon regeneration to approximately half of normal levels: only 39% and 36% of axons regenerated in parg-1 and parg-2 mutants, respectively, while 70% of axons regenerated in control animals (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments quantified in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Loss of parg-2 reduced axon regeneration to 36% compared to 70% in control animals.
source: Loss of either parg-1 or parg-2 reduced axon regeneration to approximately half of normal levels: only 39% and 36% of axons regenerated in parg-1 and parg-2 mutants, respectively, while 70% of axons regenerated in control animals (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments quantified in Figure 1E,F.

claim: parg-1 and parg-2 regulate axon regeneration.
source: Therefore, parg-1 and parg-2 regulate axon regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from axon regeneration data showing reduced regeneration in parg-1 and parg-2 mutants.

claim: The parg-1(lf); parg-2(lf) double mutant was viable and displayed wild-type morphology and behavior, indicating PARG function is not essential.
source: The resulting parg-1(lf); parg-2(lf) double mutant was viable and displayed wild-type morphology and behavior, indicating PARG function is not essential.
evidence: Supported by observations of parg-1(lf); parg-2(lf) double mutant animals.

claim: Axon regeneration in parg-1(lf); parg-2(lf) animals was similar to axon regeneration in either parg-1 or parg-2 mutant animals.
source: Axon regeneration in parg-1(lf); parg-2(lf) animals was similar to axon regeneration in either parg-1 or parg-2 mutant animals (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments quantified in Figure 1F.

claim: PARG activity is required for normal axon regeneration, but some regeneration occurs even in animals that completely lack parg.
source: Thus, PARG activity is required for normal axon regeneration, but some regeneration occurs even in animals that completely lack parg.
evidence: Inferred from regeneration data showing reduced but not eliminated regeneration in parg-1(lf); parg-2(lf) double mutants.

claim: 87% of injured axons regenerated in parg-1 mutants with GABA neuron-specific parg-1 expression restored.
source: We found that 87% and 85% of injured axons regenerated in parg-1 and parg-2 worms whose GABA neurons had restored PARG expression (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments in transgenic rescue animals quantified in Figure 1H.

claim: 85% of injured axons regenerated in parg-2 mutants with GABA neuron-specific parg-2 expression restored.
source: We found that 87% and 85% of injured axons regenerated in parg-1 and parg-2 worms whose GABA neurons had restored PARG expression (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments in transgenic rescue animals quantified in Figure 1H.

claim: Cell-intrinsic PARG function is required for axon regeneration of GABA neurons.
source: We conclude cell-intrinsic PARG function is required for axon regeneration of GABA neurons (Figure 1I).
evidence: Inferred from cell-specific rescue experiments showing restoration of regeneration with GABA neuron-specific PARG expression.

claim: Cellular levels of PARylation are determined by the balance between the activity of PARGs, which remove PAR, and the activity of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs), which add poly(ADP-ribose) to proteins.
source: Cellular levels of PARylation are determined by the balance between the activity of PARGs, which remove PAR, and the activity of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs), which transfer PAR onto target proteins (Schreiber et al., 2006; Gibson and Kraus, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Schreiber et al., 2006; Gibson and Kraus, 2012).

claim: The C. elegans genome contains two PARP homologs, parp-1 and parp-2.
source: The C. elegans genome contains two PARP homologs, parp-1 and parp-2 (Gagnon et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gagnon et al., 2002.

claim: Mutation of parp-1 increased axon regeneration to 92% compared to 76% in control animals.
source: We found that mutation of either parp-1 or parp-2 increased axon regeneration relative to control animals: 92% and 90% of axons regenerated in parp-1 and parp-2 mutants, respectively, while 76% of axons in controls regenerated (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments quantified in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Mutation of parp-2 increased axon regeneration to 90% compared to 76% in control animals.
source: We found that mutation of either parp-1 or parp-2 increased axon regeneration relative to control animals: 92% and 90% of axons regenerated in parp-1 and parp-2 mutants, respectively, while 76% of axons in controls regenerated (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments quantified in Figure 2A,B.

claim: 56% of regenerating axons in parp-1 mutants regrew at least 3/4 of the distance between the ventral and the dorsal nerve cords compared to only 26% in controls.
source: We found that 56% and 53% of regenerating axons in parp-1 and parp-2 mutants, respectively, regrew at least 3/4 of the distance between the ventral and the dorsal nerve cords compared to only 26% of regenerating axons in controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments measuring regeneration distance quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: 53% of regenerating axons in parp-2 mutants regrew at least 3/4 of the distance between the ventral and the dorsal nerve cords compared to only 26% in controls.
source: We found that 56% and 53% of regenerating axons in parp-1 and parp-2 mutants, respectively, regrew at least 3/4 of the distance between the ventral and the dorsal nerve cords compared to only 26% of regenerating axons in controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments measuring regeneration distance quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: Some parp-2 mutants sprouted new axons from the cell body.
source: Moreover, some parp-2 mutants sprouted new axons from the cell body (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The opposing effects of PARGs and PARPs on poly(ADP)-ribose and on axon regeneration indicate that PARylation is a critical determinant of regenerative potential.
source: The opposing effects of PARGs and PARPs on poly(ADP)-ribose and on axon regeneration indicate that PARylation is a critical determinant of regenerative potential.
evidence: Inferred from opposing effects of PARG and PARP mutations on axon regeneration.

claim: Axons exposed to PARP1 shRNA regenerated significantly better than axons exposed to control shRNA.
source: We found that axons exposed to PARP1 shRNA regenerated significantly better than axons exposed to control shRNA (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Supported by cortical neuron regeneration assay data quantified in Figure 2F,G.

claim: PARP was significantly reduced in neurons exposed to either of the PARP1-targeting shRNAs compared to negative control shRNA.
source: PARP was significantly reduced in neurons exposed to either of the PARP1-targeting shRNAs compared to negative control shRNA (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: Supported by western blot data quantified in Figure 2H,I.

claim: PARP-1 and PARylation are conserved inhibitors of axon regeneration after injury, and reducing their function improves axon regeneration across species.
source: Therefore, PARP-1 and PARylation are conserved inhibitors of axon regeneration after injury, and reducing their function improves axon regeneration across species.
evidence: Inferred from data showing PARP inhibition improves regeneration in both C. elegans and mammalian neurons.

claim: Loss of both parg-1 and parg-2 function reduced regeneration in the dlk-1(OE) background.
source: We found that loss of both parg-1 and parg-2 function reduced regeneration in the dlk-1(OE) background, just as loss of parg-1 and parg-2 reduces regeneration in animals with wild type levels of DLK signaling (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments in dlk-1(OE); parg-1(lf) parg-2(lf) animals quantified in Figure 2J.

claim: DLK-dependent regeneration depends in part on parg-1 and parg-2.
source: Thus, DLK-dependent regeneration depends in part on parg-1 and parg-2.
evidence: Inferred from data showing parg loss of function reduces regeneration in dlk-1(OE) background.

claim: Loss of all PARG activity did not affect synapse morphology.
source: Loss of all PARG activity did not affect synapse morphology.
evidence: Supported by analysis of SYD-2::GFP distribution in parg-1(lf) parg-2(lf) mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: Increased DLK signaling in dlk-1(OE) animals causes synapse morphology defects.
source: Increased DLK signaling in dlk-1(OE) animals causes synapse morphology defects (Figure 3) (Nakata et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 3 and citation to Nakata et al., 2005.

claim: Loss of PARG activity did not suppress synapse morphology defects caused by dlk-1(OE).
source: However, loss of PARG activity did not suppress these defects.
evidence: Supported by analysis of SYD-2::GFP distribution in dlk-1(OE); parg-1(lf) parg-2(lf) animals shown in Figure 3.

claim: In contrast to its role in axon regeneration, PARylation does not regulate synapse formation, even when DLK signaling is activated.
source: Together, these data indicate that in contrast to its role in axon regeneration, PARylation does not regulate synapse formation, even when DLK signaling is activated.
evidence: Inferred from data showing PARG loss does not affect synapse morphology in wild type or dlk-1(OE) backgrounds.

claim: PARylation is a short-lived modification, and PAR levels are normally maintained by the continuous activity of PARP and PARG proteins.
source: PARylation is a short-lived modification, and PAR levels are normally maintained by the continuous activity of PARP and PARG proteins (Schreiber et al., 2006; Gibson and Kraus, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Schreiber et al., 2006; Gibson and Kraus, 2012).

claim: Treatment with chemical PARP inhibitors after injury resulted in significantly enhanced axon regeneration in vivo in C. elegans GABA neurons.
source: We found that treatment with chemical PARP inhibitors after injury resulted in significantly enhanced axon regeneration in vivo in C. elegans GABA neurons and in vitro in murine cortical neurons (Figure 4A–C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by laser axotomy experiments with PARP inhibitor treatment quantified in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Treatment with chemical PARP inhibitors after injury resulted in significantly enhanced axon regeneration in vitro in murine cortical neurons.
source: We found that treatment with chemical PARP inhibitors after injury resulted in significantly enhanced axon regeneration in vivo in C. elegans GABA neurons and in vitro in murine cortical neurons (Figure 4A–C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cortical neuron regeneration assay with PARP inhibitor treatment quantified in Figure 4C.

claim: Drug treatment post-injury improved behavioral recovery, demonstrating that enhanced regeneration after PARP inhibition results in functional reconnection.
source: Drug treatment post-injury also improved behavioral recovery, demonstrating that enhanced regeneration after PARP inhibition results in functional reconnection (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data quantified in Figure 4D,E showing improved touch response after PARP inhibitor treatment.

claim: Acute poly(ADP-ribose) levels determine the response of neurons to axon injury.
source: Thus, acute poly(ADP-ribose) levels determine the response of neurons to axon injury, and inhibition of PARP after injury is sufficient to improve regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from data showing PARP inhibition after injury improves regeneration.

claim: Inhibition of PARP after injury is sufficient to improve regeneration.
source: Thus, acute poly(ADP-ribose) levels determine the response of neurons to axon injury, and inhibition of PARP after injury is sufficient to improve regeneration.
evidence: Supported by data showing PARP inhibitor treatment after injury improves regeneration.

claim: Regulation of PARylation is an important component of the DLK pathway role in the axon regeneration mechanism.
source: Together, our findings suggest that regulation of PARylation is an important component of the DLK pathway role in the axon regeneration mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing DLK regulates parg expression and PARylation affects regeneration.

claim: Both of the parg genes are upregulated in animals with activated DLK signaling.
source: First, we find both of the parg genes are upregulated in animals with activated DLK signaling.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data showing upregulation of parg-1 and parg-2 in dlk-1(OE).

claim: Endogenous dlk-1 signaling drives parg-2 expression in an injury-dependent manner.
source: Second, we find that endogenous dlk-1 signaling drives parg-2 expression in an injury-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by reporter expression data showing increased parg-2 promoter activity after injury in a dlk-1-dependent manner.

claim: Loss of the parg genes reduces regeneration, both in animals with endogenous levels of dlk-1 activity and in animals with elevated DLK-1 signaling.
source: Third, we find that loss of the parg genes reduces regeneration, both in animals with endogenous levels of dlk-1 activity and in animals with elevated DLK-1 signaling.
evidence: Supported by regeneration data in parg mutants in wild type and dlk-1(OE) backgrounds.

claim: DLK signaling induces parg expression, which in turn facilitates regeneration by removing PAR.
source: These findings suggest a linear model in which DLK signaling induces parg expression, which in turn facilitates regeneration by removing PAR.
evidence: Inferred from data showing DLK regulates parg expression and PARGs promote regeneration.

claim: DLK signaling regulates regeneration upstream of multiple effectors.
source: In addition to regulating PARylation, our data indicate that DLK signaling regulates regeneration upstream of multiple effectors.
evidence: Inferred from data showing some regeneration occurs in parg-1(lf) parg-2(lf) mutants but not in dlk-1(lf) mutants.

claim: Some GABA axons in parg-1(lf) parg-2(lf) mutants are still able to regenerate, indicating high levels of PAR do not completely prevent DLK-mediated axon regeneration.
source: Although PARylation has a strong effect on regeneration in both animals with wild-type levels of dlk-1 and in animals that overexpress dlk-1, some GABA axons in parg-1(lf) parg-2(lf) mutants are still able to regenerate (Figure 1F), indicating high levels of PAR do not completely prevent DLK-mediated axon regeneration.
evidence: Supported by regeneration data in Figure 1F showing partial regeneration in parg-1(lf) parg-2(lf) mutants.

claim: GABA axons do not regenerate in animals lacking DLK.
source: By contrast, GABA axons do not regenerate in animals lacking DLK (Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammarlund et al., 2009 and Yan et al., 2009.

claim: DLK activity has other functions besides regulating PARylation.
source: These data suggest that DLK activity has other functions besides regulating PARylation.
evidence: Inferred from data showing regeneration differences between parg double mutants and dlk-1 mutants.

claim: PARG and PARP activity regulate the acute response of neurons to axon injury.
source: Specifically, we find that PARG and PARP activity regulate the acute response of neurons to axon injury, and that chemical PARP inhibition after injury is sufficient to improve regeneration.
evidence: Supported by data showing PARG/PARP mutations and PARP inhibitor treatment affect regeneration after injury.

claim: Chemical PARP inhibition after injury is sufficient to improve regeneration.
source: Specifically, we find that PARG and PARP activity regulate the acute response of neurons to axon injury, and that chemical PARP inhibition after injury is sufficient to improve regeneration.
evidence: Supported by data showing PARP inhibitor treatment after injury improves regeneration.

claim: The lack of additive phenotype in the double loss of function parg-1(-); parg-2(-) mutant suggests the two parg genes are not partially redundant.
source: The lack of additive phenotype in the double loss of function parg-1(-); parg-2(-) mutant suggests the two parg genes are not partially redundant.
evidence: Inferred from regeneration data showing similar phenotypes in single and double parg mutants.

claim: parg-1 and parg-2 may function together, for example as part of a complex.
source: Rather, parg-1 and parg-2 may function together, for example as part of a complex.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of non-additive phenotype in double mutant.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, the two PARG homologs physically interact.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, the two PARG homologs physically interact (Song et al., 2015), suggesting the PARG homologs may function coordinately.
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2015.

claim: The PARG homologs may function coordinately.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, the two PARG homologs physically interact (Song et al., 2015), suggesting the PARG homologs may function coordinately.
evidence: Inferred from physical interaction data in Arabidopsis and applied to C. elegans.

claim: Concerted action of both PARGs may be required to maintain PAR levels below a threshold.
source: Alternatively, concerted action of both PARGs may be required to maintain PAR levels below a threshold.
evidence: Speculative model to explain non-additive phenotype in double mutant.

claim: Loss of either single PARG results in a sufficient PAR increase to block regeneration, but increasing PAR beyond this threshold does not further reduce regeneration.
source: In this model, loss of either single PARG results in a sufficient PAR increase to block regeneration, but increasing PAR beyond this threshold does not further reduce regeneration.
evidence: Speculative model to explain non-additive phenotype in double mutant.

claim: PARP1 is upregulated in murine cortical neurons exposed to inhibitory growth molecules (myelin-associated glycoprotein, Nogo-A, Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans) in vitro.
source: PARP1 is upregulated in murine cortical neurons exposed to inhibitory growth molecules (myelin-associated glycoprotein, Nogo-A, Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans) in vitro and in crushed optic nerves in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brochier et al., 2015 (implicit from context).

claim: PARP1 is upregulated in crushed optic nerves in vivo.
source: PARP1 is upregulated in murine cortical neurons exposed to inhibitory growth molecules (myelin-associated glycoprotein, Nogo-A, Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans) in vitro and in crushed optic nerves in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brochier et al., 2015 (implicit from context).

claim: Inhibiting PARP1 promotes neurite outgrowth on inhibitory substrates in vitro.
source: Moreover, inhibiting PARP1 promotes neurite outgrowth on inhibitory substrates in vitro (Brochier et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brochier et al., 2015.

claim: The balance between PARP and PARG function regulates axon regeneration.
source: Since PARPs and PARGs have contrasting effects on PAR levels, NAD+ levels, which are substrates of PAR (Bai, 2015), and on axon regeneration, we conclude the balance between PARP and PARG function regulates axon regeneration
evidence: Inferred from opposing effects of PARP and PARG on PAR levels and regeneration.

claim: The PARG-PARP balance may determine axon regeneration by regulating PAR levels or by regulating NAD+ levels.
source: and present the hypothesis the PARG-PARP balance may determine axon regeneration by regulating PAR levels or by regulating NAD+ levels.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about mechanism of PARG-PARP regulation of regeneration.

claim: The conservation of the role of PARP in mammalian axon regeneration may have important implications for nerve repair following injury or disease.
source: Finally, the conservation of the role of PARP in mammalian axon regeneration may have important implications for nerve repair following injury or disease.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential clinical implications based on conservation of PARP function.

claim: DLK-1 (Dual Leucine Zipper Kinase) is a mitogen activated protein kinase kinase kinase (MAPKKK) identified in C. elegans.
source: DLK-1 (Dual Leucine Zipper Kinase) is a mitogen activated protein kinase kinase kinase (MAPKKK) identified in C. elegans that functions intrinsically to regulate regeneration of adult axons in the central and peripheral nervous systems across species, including flies and mammals (Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009; Xiong et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013; Watkins et al., 2013; Byrne et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009; Xiong et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013; Watkins et al., 2013; Byrne et al., 2014).

claim: DLK-1 functions intrinsically to regulate regeneration of adult axons in the central and peripheral nervous systems across species, including flies and mammals.
source: DLK-1 (Dual Leucine Zipper Kinase) is a mitogen activated protein kinase kinase kinase (MAPKKK) identified in C. elegans that functions intrinsically to regulate regeneration of adult axons in the central and peripheral nervous systems across species, including flies and mammals (Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009; Xiong et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013; Watkins et al., 2013; Byrne et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009; Xiong et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013; Watkins et al., 2013; Byrne et al., 2014).

claim: Activation of dlk-1 enhances axon regeneration.
source: Activation of dlk-1 enhances axon regeneration and loss of dlk-1 function inhibits axon regeneration in young and aged animals (Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009; Byrne et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009; Byrne et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of dlk-1 function inhibits axon regeneration in young and aged animals.
source: Activation of dlk-1 enhances axon regeneration and loss of dlk-1 function inhibits axon regeneration in young and aged animals (Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009; Byrne et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammarlund et al., 2009; Yan et al., 2009; Byrne et al., 2014.

claim: In worms, flies, and mice, the function of DLK signaling in regeneration depends on gene transcription.
source: In worms, flies, and mice, the function of DLK signaling in regeneration depends on gene transcription (Xiong et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2012; Yan and Jin, 2012; Watkins et al., 2013; Stone et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xiong et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2012; Yan and Jin, 2012; Watkins et al., 2013; Stone et al., 2014.

claim: Specific targets of DLK transcriptional regulation may mediate the ability of DLK signaling to promote regeneration.
source: These data suggest that specific targets of DLK transcriptional regulation may mediate the ability of DLK signaling to promote regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from data showing DLK function depends on transcription.

claim: Modulation of DLK transcriptional targets might increase the intrinsic regenerative potential of injured axons.
source: Finally, modulation of these targets might increase the intrinsic regenerative potential of injured axons.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential therapeutic implications.

claim: The central nervous system does not successfully regenerate after injury, unlike damaged peripheral nerves.
source: Unlike damaged peripheral nerves, the central nervous system does not successfully regenerate after injury.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CNS vs PNS regeneration.

claim: Failure to regenerate has been attributed to two components of the regeneration response: intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
source: Failure to regenerate has been attributed to two components of the regeneration response: intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
evidence: Established framework in regeneration biology supported by citations in the following sentence.

claim: Extrinsic inhibitory factors such as the glial microenvironment can be modulated with some success, but regeneration potential is still substantially hindered, providing evidence that intrinsic factors play a significant role in modulating the ability of an axon to regenerate.
source: While extrinsic inhibitory factors such as the glial microenvironment can be modulated with some success, regeneration potential is still substantially hindered, providing evidence that intrinsic factors play a significant role in modulating the ability of an axon to regenerate (Richardson et al., 1980; Neumann and Woolf, 1999; GrandPré et al., 2000; Fournier et al., 2001; Qiu et al., 2002; Yiu and He, 2006; Park et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Richardson et al., 1980; Neumann and Woolf, 1999; GrandPré et al., 2000; Fournier et al., 2001; Qiu et al., 2002; Yiu and He, 2006; Park et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: PARGs, which remove poly(ADP-ribose) from proteins, act in injured C. elegans GABA motor neurons to enhance axon regeneration.
source: PARGs, which remove poly(ADP-ribose) from proteins, act in injured C. elegans GABA motor neurons to enhance axon regeneration.
evidence: Supported by cell-specific rescue experiments and regeneration assays in parg mutants.

claim: PARG expression is regulated by DLK signaling.
source: PARG expression is regulated by DLK signaling, and PARGs mediate DLK function in enhancing axon regeneration.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data and reporter expression analysis.

claim: PARGs mediate DLK function in enhancing axon regeneration.
source: PARG expression is regulated by DLK signaling, and PARGs mediate DLK function in enhancing axon regeneration.
evidence: Supported by genetic epistasis experiments showing parg loss reduces regeneration in dlk-1(OE) background.

claim: PARPs, which add poly(ADP-ribose) to proteins, inhibit axon regeneration of both C. elegans GABA neurons and mammalian cortical neurons.
